claim: Nervous systems distinguish between self- and other-generated movements by monitoring discrepancies between planned and performed actions.
source: Nervous systems distinguish between self- and other-generated movements by monitoring discrepancies between planned and performed actions.
evidence: This is a general statement about nervous system function presented in the abstract without specific experimental data from this manuscript, but draws on established scientific understanding.

claim: Corollary discharges are conveyed to sensory areas and gate expected reafference.
source: To do so, corollary discharges are conveyed to sensory areas and gate expected reafference.
evidence: This statement describes an established mechanism in neuroscience, presented as background knowledge.

claim: Gating of reafference is observed in neonatal rats during wake-related movements.
source: Such gating is observed in neonatal rats during wake-related movements.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental findings presented in the manuscript, particularly the data showing reduced ECN activity during wake movements.

claim: Twitches are self-generated movements produced during active (or REM) sleep.
source: In contrast, twitches, which are self-generated movements produced during active (or REM) sleep, differ from wake movements in that they reliably trigger robust neural activity.
evidence: This is a definitional statement about twitches that is supported by the experimental observations in the manuscript.

claim: Twitches reliably trigger robust neural activity.
source: In contrast, twitches, which are self-generated movements produced during active (or REM) sleep, differ from wake movements in that they reliably trigger robust neural activity.
evidence: This claim is directly supported by the experimental data showing increased neural activity in response to twitches in both SMC and ECN.

claim: The gating actions of corollary discharge are absent during twitching.
source: Accordingly, we hypothesized that the gating actions of corollary discharge are absent during twitching.
evidence: This is presented as a hypothesis that is then tested and supported by the experimental findings.

claim: The external cuneate nucleus (ECN) processes sensory input from the forelimbs.
source: Here, we identify the external cuneate nucleus (ECN), which processes sensory input from the forelimbs, as a site of movement-dependent sensory gating during wake.
evidence: This is supported by both established anatomical knowledge and the experimental findings in this manuscript.

claim: The ECN is a site of movement-dependent sensory gating during wake.
source: Here, we identify the external cuneate nucleus (ECN), which processes sensory input from the forelimbs, as a site of movement-dependent sensory gating during wake.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the manuscript, supported by the experimental data showing differential ECN activity during wake versus sleep.

claim: Pharmacological disinhibition of the ECN unmasked wake-related reafference.
source: Whereas pharmacological disinhibition of the ECN unmasked wake-related reafference, twitch-related reafference was unaffected.
evidence: This is directly supported by the experimental data showing increased ECN activity during wake movements after GABA/glycine antagonist application.

claim: Pharmacological disinhibition of the ECN did not affect twitch-related reafference.
source: Whereas pharmacological disinhibition of the ECN unmasked wake-related reafference, twitch-related reafference was unaffected.
evidence: This is directly supported by the experimental data showing no change in ECN activity during twitches after GABA/glycine antagonist application.

claim: This is the first demonstration of a neural comparator that is differentially engaged depending on the kind of movement produced.
source: This is the first demonstration of a neural comparator that is differentially engaged depending on the kind of movement produced.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the findings, which is a form of inference based on the authors' knowledge of the literature.

claim: Twitches trigger abundant reafferent activation of sensorimotor circuits in the developing brain.
source: This mechanism explains how twitches, although self-generated, trigger abundant reafferent activation of sensorimotor circuits in the developing brain.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data showing robust neural activity in response to twitches.

claim: Animals of diverse vertebrate and invertebrate species distinguish between sensations arising from self-generated movements from those arising from other-generated movements.
source: Animals of diverse vertebrate and invertebrate species distinguish between sensations arising from self-generated movements from those arising from other-generated movements (Crapse and Sommer, 2008; Sommer and Wurtz, 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Motor areas produce copies of motor commands (i.e., corollary discharges) that are directly compared with sensory signals arising from self-generated movements (i.e., reafference).
source: To make this distinction between self and other, motor areas produce copies of motor commands (i.e., corollary discharges) that are directly compared with sensory signals arising from self-generated movements (i.e., reafference; [Poulet and Hedwig 2006; Sommer and Wurtz 2002]).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: At the level of the neural comparator, reafference is blocked when there are no discrepancies between the corollary discharge and reafferent signals.
source: At the level of the neural comparator, reafference is blocked when there are no discrepancies between the corollary discharge and reafferent signals (Poulet and Hedwig 2006; Bell, 2001; Brooks and Cullen, 2014; Bell, 1989).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Expected reafference arising from voluntary movements is attenuated.
source: As a result, expected reafference arising from voluntary movements is attenuated (Voss et al., 2006; Seki et al., 2003; Haggard and Whitford 2004), thereby increasing the salience of unexpected reafference (Poulet and Hedwig 2006; Brooks et al., 2015; Brooks and Cullen, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Attenuation of expected reafference increases the salience of unexpected reafference.
source: As a result, expected reafference arising from voluntary movements is attenuated (Voss et al., 2006; Seki et al., 2003; Haggard and Whitford 2004), thereby increasing the salience of unexpected reafference (Poulet and Hedwig 2006; Brooks et al., 2015; Brooks and Cullen, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature and represents an inference about the functional consequence of reafference attenuation.

claim: Wake-related movements do not trigger substantial reafference in sensorimotor cortex (SMC) in week-old rats.
source: We previously demonstrated in week-old rats that wake-related movements do not trigger substantial reafference in sensorimotor cortex (SMC).
evidence: This claim refers to previous work by the authors and is supported by citation to their earlier study.

claim: Sleep-related twitches trigger robust reafference in sensorimotor cortex.
source: In contrast, sleep-related twitches—which are produced exclusively and abundantly during active (or REM) sleep—trigger robust reafference (Tiriac et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim refers to previous work by the authors and is supported by citation to their earlier study.

claim: Twitches are produced exclusively and abundantly during active (or REM) sleep.
source: In contrast, sleep-related twitches—which are produced exclusively and abundantly during active (or REM) sleep—trigger robust reafference (Tiriac et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a descriptive claim about twitches that is supported by established knowledge and the authors' previous work.

claim: Twitches are processed by the nervous system as if they are unexpected.
source: We provided converging evidence that twitches, unlike wake movements, are processed by the nervous system as if they are unexpected.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental findings showing robust reafference during twitches.

claim: There must be a neural structure, located somewhere within the sensorimotor network, that acts as a comparator to specifically gate wake-related reafference.
source: If true, there must be a neural structure, located somewhere within the sensorimotor network, that acts as a comparator to specifically gate wake-related reafference.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the hypothesis that corollary discharge is absent or inhibited during twitching.

claim: The ECN receives primary muscle spindle afferents from forelimb and nuchal muscles.
source: One possible comparator is the external cuneate nucleus (ECN), which receives primary muscle spindle afferents from forelimb and nuchal muscles and conveys sensory information to downstream structures including the cerebellum, thalamus, and cerebral cortex (Campbell et al., 1974; Cooke et al., 1971; Mackie et al., 1999; Boivie and Boman, 1981; Huang et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous anatomical studies.

claim: The ECN conveys sensory information to downstream structures including the cerebellum, thalamus, and cerebral cortex.
source: One possible comparator is the external cuneate nucleus (ECN), which receives primary muscle spindle afferents from forelimb and nuchal muscles and conveys sensory information to downstream structures including the cerebellum, thalamus, and cerebral cortex (Campbell et al., 1974; Cooke et al., 1971; Mackie et al., 1999; Boivie and Boman, 1981; Huang et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous anatomical studies.

claim: The ECN receives projections from the red nucleus.
source: Moreover, the ECN receives projections from such premotor structures as the red nucleus (Holstege and Tan, 1988; Edwards, 1972; Martin et al., 1974)—which contributes both to the production of wake movements and twitches in infant rats (Del Rio-Bermudez et al., 2015)—and the premotor C3-C4 propriospinal neurons (PNs; [Pivetta et al., 2014]), which have been implicated in the conveyance of corollary discharge (Pivetta et al., 2014; Alstermark et al., 2007; Azim et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous anatomical studies.

claim: The red nucleus contributes both to the production of wake movements and twitches in infant rats.
source: Moreover, the ECN receives projections from such premotor structures as the red nucleus (Holstege and Tan, 1988; Edwards, 1972; Martin et al., 1974)—which contributes both to the production of wake movements and twitches in infant rats (Del Rio-Bermudez et al., 2015)—and the premotor C3-C4 propriospinal neurons (PNs; [Pivetta et al., 2014]), which have been implicated in the conveyance of corollary discharge (Pivetta et al., 2014; Alstermark et al., 2007; Azim et al., 2014).

claim: The ECN receives projections from premotor C3-C4 propriospinal neurons (PNs).

claim: C3-C4 propriospinal neurons have been implicated in the conveyance of corollary discharge.

evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Corollary discharge from the red nucleus or PNs could contribute to sensory gating in the ECN via known GABAergic and glycinergic inputs to that structure.
source: Corollary discharge from the red nucleus or PNs could contribute to sensory gating in the ECN via known GABAergic and glycinergic inputs to that structure (Galindo and Krnjević, 1967; Heino and Westman 1991; Sato et al., 1991), perhaps through presynaptic inhibition (Seki et al., 2003; Andersen et al., 1964).
evidence: This is a speculative claim about a possible mechanism, supported by citations to previous work on GABAergic and glycinergic inputs.

claim: The ECN has GABAergic and glycinergic inputs.

claim: Sensory gating in the ECN may occur through presynaptic inhibition.

evidence: This is a speculative claim about a possible mechanism, supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The mean rate of spindle bursts was significantly higher during active sleep than during wake in the forelimb region of SMC.
source: Across all pups, the mean rate of spindle bursts (t5 = 10.2, p=0.0002, n = 6 pups) and unit activity (t7 = 3.9, p=0.006, n = 8 units) was significantly higher during active sleep than during wake (Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by statistical analysis of experimental data and is shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The mean rate of unit activity was significantly higher during active sleep than during wake in the forelimb region of SMC.
source: Across all pups, the mean rate of spindle bursts (t5 = 10.2, p=0.0002, n = 6 pups) and unit activity (t7 = 3.9, p=0.006, n = 8 units) was significantly higher during active sleep than during wake (Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by statistical analysis of experimental data and is shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Spindle bursts and unit activity were triggered by forelimb twitches with a latency of 100–125 ms.
source: Moreover, spindle bursts and unit activity were triggered by forelimb twitches with a latency of 100–125 ms (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by the event correlation analysis shown in Figure 1C.

claim: ECN firing rate was higher in response to forelimb twitches than to hindlimb twitches.
source: As expected, ECN firing rate was higher in response to forelimb twitches than to hindlimb (t8 = 3.5, p=0.008) or nuchal (t21 = 3.2, p=0.007) twitches (Figure 2B)
evidence: This claim is directly supported by statistical analysis of experimental data and is shown in Figure 2B.

claim: ECN firing rate was higher in response to forelimb twitches than to nuchal twitches.
source: As expected, ECN firing rate was higher in response to forelimb twitches than to hindlimb (t8 = 3.5, p=0.008) or nuchal (t21 = 3.2, p=0.007) twitches (Figure 2B)
evidence: This claim is directly supported by statistical analysis of experimental data and is shown in Figure 2B.

claim: There was no significant difference in ECN firing rate between hindlimb and nuchal twitches.
source: there was no significant difference in ECN firing rate between hindlimb and nuchal twitches (t8 = 1.3, p=0.23).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: The latency to twitch-related ECN activity (10–50 ms) was shorter than that observed in SMC (100–125 ms).
source: Also, as expected given the relative anatomical locations of the ECN and SMC, the latency to twitch-related ECN activity (10–50 ms) was shorter than that observed in SMC (100–125 ms; see Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of experimental data from ECN and SMC recordings, with reference to Figure 1C.

claim: ECN firing rate was movement dependent, with greater activity occurring during periods of forelimb twitching than during periods of forelimb wake movement.
source: Finally, ECN firing rate was movement dependent, with greater activity occurring during periods of forelimb twitching than during periods of forelimb wake movement (t15 = 2.8, p=0.012, Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by statistical analysis of experimental data and is shown in Figure 2C.

claim: There was no significant effect of behavioral state on ECN activity in response to forelimb stimulation.
source: As shown in Figure 2D, there was no significant effect of behavioral state on ECN activity in response to forelimb stimulation (t5 = 1.2, p=0.286).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by statistical analysis of experimental data and is shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The lack of state-dependent difference in ECN response to forelimb stimulation is consistent with earlier findings in the hindlimb region of SMC.
source: This result is consistent with our earlier finding in the hindlimb region of SMC (Tiriac et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim connects the current findings to previous work by citation.

claim: Inhibitory blockade of the ECN unmasked reafference in response to forelimb wake movements.
source: As predicted, inhibitory blockade of the ECN unmasked reafference in response to forelimb wake movements (t8 = 3.7 p=0.006, Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by statistical analysis of experimental data and is shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Inhibitory blockade had no effect on ECN reafference in response to forelimb twitches.
source: Moreover, and again as predicted, inhibitory blockade had no effect on ECN reafference in response to forelimb twitches (Figure 3D).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Saline infusions had no effect on either wake or sleep reafference.
source: Saline infusions had no effect on either wake or sleep reafference.
evidence: This claim is supported by the control experiment data.

claim: Blocking GABAA and glycine receptors had no effect on the amplitude of wake movements.
source: Blocking GABAA and glycine receptors had no effect on the amplitude of wake movements (Figure 4A), the frequency of forelimb wake movements (Figure 4B), or the frequency of forelimb twitches (Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Blocking GABAA and glycine receptors had no effect on the frequency of forelimb wake movements.
source: Blocking GABAA and glycine receptors had no effect on the amplitude of wake movements (Figure 4A), the frequency of forelimb wake movements (Figure 4B), or the frequency of forelimb twitches (Figure 4C).

claim: Blocking GABAA and glycine receptors had no effect on the frequency of forelimb twitches.

claim: Inhibitory blockade had no effect on tonic neural activity in the ECN.
source: Moreover, inhibitory blockade had no effect on tonic neural activity in the ECN (Figure 4D), thus providing further evidence that the inhibitory inputs to the ECN function specifically in the context of wake movements.

claim: The inhibitory inputs to the ECN function specifically in the context of wake movements.
source: Moreover, inhibitory blockade had no effect on tonic neural activity in the ECN (Figure 4D), thus providing further evidence that the inhibitory inputs to the ECN function specifically in the context of wake movements.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental finding that inhibitory blockade only affected wake-related reafference.

claim: The ECN is a sensory structure.
source: First, to be a comparator, the ECN must be a sensory structure; in fact, the ECN processes proprioceptive inputs from forelimb and nuchal muscles (Campbell et al., 1974) and recordings from anesthetized cats have demonstrated that the ECN codes, with high fidelity, the stretch on muscle fibers (Mackie et al., 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous anatomical and physiological studies.

claim: The ECN processes proprioceptive inputs from forelimb and nuchal muscles.

claim: Inhibitory blockade of the ECN had no effect on the ECN's tonic firing rate.

claim: Premotor structures like the red nucleus may be state-dependently modulated such that they convey motor copies to the ECN (or an intervening structure) only during wake movements.
source: Therefore, it may be that (a) premotor structures like the red nucleus are state-dependently modulated such that they convey motor copies to the ECN (or an intervening structure) only during wake movements, or (b) the ECN receives motor copies from both types of movements, but state-dependent modulation of the ECN prevents the twitch-related motor copies from engaging the inhibitory mechanism.
evidence: This is a speculative claim about possible mechanisms to explain the findings.
